speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head O of the Estimates be reduced by $100." I declare that I am a medical doctor in a public hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the Budget debate, I spoke on "stress tests" for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we also need to prepare our healthcare system for tomorrow, test our plans for the future before the future tests us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak on three areas today: better care for an ageing population, amidst better care coordination, better access to treatments and better support for our healthcare workers and frontliners.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I asked a Written Question in Parliament early this year: how many Specialist Outpatient Clinic (SOC) visits a patient might have in a single year in our public hospitals?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Here are MOH's figures from 2019, before COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is 7,000 patients averaging two or more clinic visits a month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is 2,000 patients, each averaging three or more clinic visits a month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If you are less mobile, it might mean having to take a taxi.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If you are still working, it might mean time away from work.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For caregivers, time commitment, too, and not every employer is supportive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And for some low-income, daily-rated workers, each clinic visit means loss of income.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met Clementi residents, worried about this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But they also see how busy our healthcare workers are across Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And yet, without enough time, space, opportunity to fully coordinate the care, it is hard to reduce and simplify the number of visits and appointments and journeys across multiple medical teams when a patient has multiple medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I raised this back in 2009 in the Singapore Medical Association Newsletter – the SMA News.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It recognises that coordination is important, adds value in and of itself beyond a single specialisation, beyond a single Ministry.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, there is a role for the coordinating physician, someone who has walked with you for years, knows the ins and outs of your medical journey throughout your journey as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when the situation is complex, someone that can be a bridge between different specialists, different medical teams, not taking the place of individual experts, but bringing that holistic view, working with you, for you, for your health and your care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But ultimately, it is a role that requires deep knowledge of the patient, deep understanding of the patient, a certain breadth of medical experience and, most importantly, depth of wisdom.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is high-value work, it takes time, it takes effort and it should be appropriately recognised and supported throughout the healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it would have been even harder without the help and support of our family physicians and our GPs in the community, on the community frontlines, supporting patients, helping patients recover in the community, to help reduce the brunt of the COVID-19 wave at our acute hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I know some family physicians, including in Clementi, some are themselves not young and faced significant personal risk in looking patients in the early days the pandemic especially, before there were vaccinations against COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have also asked about support, closer collaboration with our hospitals, in peacetime and in crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And this means we need to find ways to support and empower our family physicians and GPs better, help healthcare clusters and family doctors connect to work together more closely, make it easier for information to flow and be shared to build that understanding of how best to care for a patient – so that care can be better coordinated even amidst an ageing population and patients with more complex medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Quitting smoking, lifestyle changes, challenging conversations in a health crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These are not just KPIs or targets or policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each healthcare worker has but 24 hours a day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet, our time is one of the most precious gifts we can give to a patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And decision makers and planners need to get even better at understanding how much time it takes to deliver quality care – whether face-to-face in clinic; on the telephone or through video-conference, including after hours; connecting with different patient care stakeholders, different medical teams; coordinating, improving a patient's journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because it is only when decision-makers deeply understand what is needed, that planning and policy can be implemented in a way that does the most good.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even the best pilot needs to know what is the air speed, what is the altitude, how much fuel in the tank.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, there are computers everywhere in healthcare but we know that the computer systems can be improved, made easier to use.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Those 14 million minutes could have helped our healthcare workers connect better with patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Building a care relationship to help someone stop smoking, or forging that trust through a healthcare journey, that trust which is needed in a mental health situation or when there is a life-changing diagnosis, a health crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every minute matters when there are many, many people sick, needing urgent care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, work spaces, IT user interface – not a small matter.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must give it the same attention and focus on policy and implementation that the big firms, like Apple and Google do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have seen that GovTech can develop best-in-class user interface: simple, elegant, gets the job done.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Parking.sg – a small app but it shows we do have these capabilities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Should we also have a higher ambition, designing and building our own homegrown national IT healthcare platform, best-in-class, competitive or better than what is available internationally?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As easy to use as an Apple or Google app, built by Singaporeans, for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if we build something that good, we know that we can sell it to the world as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can CHAS and Outpatient MediSave be streamlined further, access improved?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In September 2020, I had spoken about this, how individual patients, individual consumers do not have the bargaining power to take on an insurer, even when there are asymmetric terms and conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How the invisible hand of the market can become unbalanced and sometimes, you need the visible hand of the regulator to put things right on an even playing field.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But surely if a doctor is fit and proper for Company A, presumably they are fit and proper as well for Company B?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On better medication prices, I also asked how we can ensure affordable access to new treatments, like cell-based therapies?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether we can have cheaper, equally effective medications competing in the Singapore market amidst our Free Trade Agreements and intellectual property regulations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: More than two years, working guts out – day in, day out.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On our nurses and our allied health sisters and brothers, I previously called upon MOH to look at paying our nurses more.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, I call upon this Government to do a deep review – see what more can be done, because how we budget, how we formulate manpower policy, it is not just a question of market forces.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It speaks to the values we have, what we hold dear and to the direction and message we want to send for our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Parliamentary Questions and in last year's Budget debate, I asked about outsourced healthcare workers serving on COVID-19 frontlines, in our COVID-19 wards, same patient care area, same risk, facing the same virus.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because every worker matters, including outsourced workers, because in a pandemic, the virus does not ask to read your contract terms and conditions before deciding whether to infect you.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to continue looking at this and continue improving.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also want to speak up for our young doctors who do long hours, long shifts on call.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This can mean working a full day, sometimes starting at 6.00 am, sometimes earlier, working the whole night and working for a significant part of the next day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today's patients are more sick, more complex than when I was a houseman many years ago.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is also a much heavier load of electronic records, electronic messages, administrative loads as well for our young junior doctors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need again, Mr Speaker, to seek truth from facts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know in America, their house officers, their interns are more likely to have a motor vehicle accident at the end of a long shift.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are hospital near-misses more likely to happen towards the end of the shift?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does a night shift system change the pattern of near-misses?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The aviation industry, militaries around the world have studied the impact of sleep deprivation for many years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can learn from this and see how we can improve safety and patient care in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also want to speak up for healthcare workers who are caregivers at home, nurses who, after a long shift looking after very ill patients, return home and have to care for a parent who is ill with dementia, a parent who is herself or himself needing care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, first I would like to declare my role as a consultant in healthcare transformation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is an important line of defence and primary care family physicians play a very critical role in caring for patients for non-emergency needs, preventing acute hospital episodes where possible, especially seen during this COVID-19 pandemic period.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many developed countries around the world attempt to provide proactive primary health services instead of reactive care where a person will only visit a doctor when they are sick.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This practice shifts the focus from treatment of acute and chronic diseases to disease prevention and early management.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With our chronic disease prevalence continuing to rise with our rapidly ageing population, this form of comprehensive primary care delivery may be beneficial for our population for several reasons.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, early screening and diagnosis can also help in better management of chronic diseases, rendering it more cost-effective in the long term by avoiding complications and reducing needs for hospitalised care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A point to note is that to anchor health delivery in the primary care and activating more GPs to engage in preventive and chronic disease management, GPs will have to assume more responsibility for the long-term health and well-being of their patients that they are serving.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is likely to have additional workload for GPs as they would now have to monitor and provide follow-up care for more.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially important to note, as we know that many GPs have already stretched themselves to support the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, primary care is the first line of defence in the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: General Practitioners (GPs) are critical to the care landscape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not only can they help to alleviate pressure on the public healthcare system, as they have demonstrated during the pandemic, they are also important for chronic disease management, especially for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One of the main roles of GPs is to identify the need for specialist care and to refer patients accordingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For holistic care, GPs should also connect patients to social service agencies for social interventions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, if they need to exercise or to take part in interest groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry intend to activate the GPs in these areas?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we better connect the GPs to the various social services in the community?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In countries like Sweden and Norway, each family is assigned to a GP of their choice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is ideal for health management, because a good doctor-patient relationship plays a significant role in fostering trust in patients to accept healthcare advice and to adopt good healthcare practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, some patients have the tendency to doctor-hop.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A possible reason could be that different GPs have different rest days and opening hours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, I would like to take this opportunity to express my appreciation to our GPs for stepping up during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, it was Benjamin Franklin who said: "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: He said it nearly 300 years ago, but it still holds true today.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I fully agree with the Minister that preventive healthcare is critical.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, one of the main incentive of encouraging Singaporeans to maintain a healthy lifestyle is to give vouchers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the private sector, at least one insurance company allows healthy members to enjoy insurance benefits, like additional coverage or premium discounts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If you want to prevent the steep escalation of healthcare costs by three times over the next 10 years, we need to go upstream to persuade Singaporeans to live a healthy lifestyle so as to maximise their chances of having more years of healthy living and quality living in their twilight years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Beyond e-vouchers, I suggest we could incentivise Singaporeans to exercise regularly, eat healthily and take the appropriate vaccines by giving discounts on the CareShield Life Insurance premium, that means, giving a discount to the premium that we all have to pay.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And give a discount to the medical cost during visits to polyclinics and public hospitals for treatment as well as for medical check-ups.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The discount given can be tiered according to the level of achievement based on clear KPIs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This may mean that we have to increase the budget for preventive healthcare because of all these discounts and incentives given.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But such investments are worthy, especially if we can significantly reduce the pace of increase of medical cost over the next decade.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Next, we need to limit the intake of sugar and salt.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Could MOH provide an update on the result of the war against sugar?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Does MOH have a similar plan to wage a war against salt as well?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In summary, I concur with the need to encourage healthy living.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In particular, we need to allocate more resources to preventive healthcare and the efforts to keep our Singaporeans healthy very significantly, at least in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thereafter, we can adjust the investment into preventive healthcare.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as a practising eye doctor in the private sector.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The adage "Prevention is better than cure" still holds true and is even more relevant today as we face rapidly increasing healthcare costs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Many of us take health for granted and only start to regret when we lose it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Those who own a car will know the importance of preventive maintenance for their beloved cars but how many of these drivers actually do preventive health for themselves?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It is especially challenging when someone feels, “Why do I need to spend the money or the time, or worry about my health when I am feeling alright?” Little do they appreciate and, often, until it is too late, that preventive healthcare means catching potential problems before they become real big problems.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Many do not realise that it is more cost effective to do regular preventive health checks than to seek help when a problem arises.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the response to MOH’s various health screening programmes and campaigns in the past five years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In what areas of preventive health is MOH going to focus on?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the longer-term plan for preventive health for a healthier Singaporean population?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What can be done to encourage and promote preventive health in our community?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Has any study been done to understand the reasons why people generally avoid preventive healthcare?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can Government put more subsidies into preventive health to make it more accessible and affordable to all Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Currently, there are insurance companies who incentivised their insured to practise good and safe driving habits using various apps and offering discounts to the premiums for renewal and also offer e-vouchers for the insured to adopt healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can MOH consider more similar incentives to Singaporeans to encourage them to embrace preventive health?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Perhaps Government can offer a discount to our MediShield and CareShield premiums as incentives for those who adopt regular health screening and healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We all have heard the saying on the ground that "one can die but cannot afford to be sick".

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Healthcare costs and affordability is a real concern for many as our population ages rapidly.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the Government doing to slow down the rise of healthcare expenses?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What are the main drivers of rapidly rising healthcare costs in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What can Singaporeans expect to see in our healthcare infrastructures and services in a decade from now?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When we discuss healthcare financing, our famous 3Ms healthcare financing framework comes to mind – our current MediSave, MediSheid and MediFund.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When was the last time we refined, or changed or augmented our current framework?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Will we see an increase in our MediSave contribution rates, an increase in MediSave limit and an increase in our MediShield premiums as healthcare costs increase?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: To help Singaporeans cope with healthcare costs, especially those with chronic illnesses, can the Government raise the MediSave limit we can use for both inpatient as well as outpatient for these diseases?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the MediSave limit be relaxed for those who are older, especially for those who have significant savings in their CPF MediSave account?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: They always lament that "I have money in my MediSave account, why do I need to use my hard-earned cash to pay for my medical bills, as I stretch my dollar?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: So, with that, I hope the Government can continue to work towards a healthier Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, our healthcare workforce needs to transform to accelerate the implementation of the "3 Beyonds" strategy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, putting in place the organisation enablers to support the shifts in the "3 Beyonds" – how to manage the workforce across the public and private healthcare system in the new healthcare delivery model and increase their productivity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Doctors, GPs, nurses, pharmacists and more in the community will play new roles and need to be empowered with new skills, capabilities, evidence‐based practices and tools, as we move beyond hospital to the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we move beyond quality to value, behavioural shifts are needed across the system, from the hospital CEO to frontliners.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we shift beyond healthcare to health, new skills will be needed, such as in data analytics and behavioural economics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Across the board, new ways of working – much more multi-disciplinary, much more agile, will be needed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This means putting in place the right organisational structures, achieving clarity of roles and responsibilities, aligning funding models, KPIs and incentives, and bringing in and building the right talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister share what the Government is doing to facilitate this transformation?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, the work of healthcare worker needs to be re-imagined digitally as we move to increasingly digital integrated care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: New digital roles will be needed in data analytics and AI, in robotics and they will need to be brought in from outside.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But importantly, all healthcare workers, will need to embrace digital skills and adopt a digital mindset, seeing digital as an enabler rather than a threat.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What forms of digital reskilling and upskilling programmes are being developed to help our healthcare professionals pivot to the digital future of healthcare?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Nurses are the bedrock of our healthcare workforce.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The burden of the pandemic has without a doubt, been felt most keenly by our tired nurses.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With an ageing population, increasing life expectancy and increasing incidence of chronic diseases, the demand for nurses can only continue in intensity and nursing care required will also increase.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we shift beyond hospital care to community care, nurses will be needed not only in hospitals but also in the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I echo the hon Member Dr Tan Wu Meng's point that more needs to be done to raise the standing of the nursing profession and further review of remuneration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Those are calls for rationality and pragmatism in addressing the foreign nurses who complement our pool.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The shortage of nurses is a global one.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a need to broaden the definition of a healthcare worker, where someone who has good interpersonal skills and motivational skills, and with technology, can play a key role in population health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is also scope to increase diversity in leadership, including in cluster leadership, to better reflect the population we serve and the skills and backgrounds required in the new healthcare model.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: There is an urgent need to transform to keep our healthcare costs in check.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we hope the Minister will not forget what he said at that virtual media conference, that these rules, meaning the COVID-19 rules, accumulated over the past two years have become quite unwieldy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, we need to review and streamline many of these rules and the most unwieldy of these must surely be the vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS) introduced incrementally from July 2021, when we switched to the living with COVD-19 strategy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has brought significant misery to a number of Singaporeans who have valid personal reasons not to vaccinate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfortunately, up till today, many of these VDS are still enforced, never mind that other rules have been relaxed with the arrival of the dominant but less virulent Omicron strain.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The vaccines reduce the severity of COVID-19 infection, but they have generally fallen short in their touted efficacy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vaccination was not the universal panacea we imagined and had little impact in reducing both infection rate and a spread of the virus, especially with the current Omicron variant.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we move forward towards normalcy in 2022, we urge the Government to relax all its discrimination policies based on vaccination status.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The relevance and justification for VDS have dwindled and I believe the general public does not view this as being favourable or fair.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans who are unvaccinated are genuinely concerned about their health and each has valid concerns about the vaccine.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their movements continue to be restrained and some had to give up their right to employment due to such restrictions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, parents too, have to contend with stress over vaccinations for their children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And there is a growing number of vaccinated Singaporeans agonising over the issue of booster shots.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is of particular concern and warrants closer scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One case of severe reaction compromising a child's health, going forward, is one case too many, given the fact that children are largely spared from any adverse health challenges from COVID-19 infection.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time for the Government to show its magnanimity to this small group of unvaccinated people by relaxing the VDS and not continue to punish them for making rational personal choices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are not troublemakers as the Government seems to make them out to be.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, the Government should focus its resources on approving more therapeutics for GPs to treat patients, to deal with the surge and infections.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are especially concerned about the senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the last two years, we have established that age is the most important determinant in risk factors leading to death.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, management of the senior COVID-19 patient can be more targeted.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We see hope in Omicron being a game changer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us review and refine our measures in our fight against COVID-19 and emerge as a people that is more compassionate and united than ever.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare pecuniary interest as a breast surgeon in private practice and as the elected president of Singapore Medical Association (SMA).

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I spoke on the difficulties faced by patients in the fair utilisation of their Integrated Shield Plans.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that the Multilateral Healthcare Insurance Committee (MHIC), of which I am a member, has made some progress in this area over the past year.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I would like to share my views on the limitations of Employee Benefit (EB) plans, also commonly known as corporate insurance, or company insurance; the influence of Third Party Administrators (TPAs) and concierge services.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These last two arose out of an apparent need to provide a gap in services and, like any other businesses, they charge.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But how do they charge, who do they charge and who regulates them?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: To give the background, healthcare economics is incredibly complex, with seven Shield Plan providers, multiple types of insurance products, numerous insurance companies offering EB plans, private hospitals, day surgery centres, close to 2,000 private specialists, 3,000 GPs, multiple radiology centres and labs and all with different business models.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: TPAs and concierges are, perhaps, the natural result of market needs and forces.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For any company offering health benefits, the administration needed to manage employees’ healthcare claims may be deemed too tedious or not cost-effective to be done in-house by their Human Resources team.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In the most idealistic form, concierge groups help patients to find doctors suitable for their conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some patients would go by friends' or families’ recommendations, some ask their GPs, some would check their Shield Plan panel list, some would google and do their own research – but some, some would use concierge services.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I know that the SMC Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines (ECEG) has clearly stated that fee-splitting is wrong, but the ECEG applies only to doctors.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The onus is on us to be aware of the fees and not to fall foul of our ethical code.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some say that one simple solution is for doctors to refuse to sign any TPA or concierge agreements.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But it may not be possible for a doctor to refuse to sign on any of these, depending on the location and model of their practice.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A robust private sector complements the restructured services.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The unity of the various healthcare sectors in rising up to the unprecedented challenge of COVID-19 is a matter of public record.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The private primary care sector has answered the call of MOH, in the Public Health Preparedness Clinics and Swab and Send Home clinics.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As awkward as it is to talk about money, fair reimbursement is necessary for a sustainable business model.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As president of SMA, I have received feedback on what sounds like grossly unfair reimbursements by TPAs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Most TPAs often have limits or caps on medications and some GPs have taken the loss on themselves if they want to provide an adequate course of medications for the patient, for example, the duration of antibiotics.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This may result in a compromise of good patient care when doctors are not adequately reimbursed.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The ongoing Fullerton case reported in The Business Times in January this year left some doctors wondering if they will ever receive their fair pay.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: GP clinics meet 80% of the primary care demand.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: They are our first line of care for the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: GP clinics are not just sources of income for doctors, they are also places where nurses and administrative staff are gainfully employed.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: TPAs may be the main source of income for many private clinics and I fear that the livelihoods of many will end up being held hostage to the unilateral pressures of the larger and financially stronger TPAs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We should not allow the livelihoods of private healthcare workers to be lost in the name of turning a profit.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I ask for MOH and MOM to consider this in the year ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My vision is that SMA continues to be the bridge between doctors and patients, doctors and insurers, doctors and the Government, to achieve an equitable healthcare ecosystem for doctors and for patients.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Minister for Health announced that we would be ready with 1,000 ICU beds, a figure that was subsequently clarified, it remained unclear what the plan was to ramp up ICU bed capacity without the degradation in the standard of care, in preparation for an endemic COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I asked a Parliamentary Question on ICU bed capacity last year and the response received was that we should avoid getting near or needing 1,000 beds and to focus on stabilising COVID-19 case counts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the points made subsequently about the trade-offs in the standard of care if a large number of ICU beds have to be stood up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this still does not get to the meat of the matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, what specific preparations were made for the recruitment of healthcare manpower in step with preparations for endemicity, as announced by the MTF in late June 2021?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Foreign healthcare workers also resigned in bigger numbers especially as they were unable to travel to see their family back home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I asked the Senior Minister of State at the same Sitting in a supplementary question what were the recruitment rates of healthcare manpower over the same period; what efforts, if any, were taken in the middle of last year in step with the transition to COVID-19 endemicity, to recruit foreign manpower on an exceptional or an urgent basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if, for example, the training of new foreign manpower to complement local healthcare workers would take some time, it would, nonetheless, have played an important part in reducing the load on our healthcare workers in time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More generally, a labour shortfall in the public healthcare sector also appears to persist in recent weeks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The stresses on our healthcare workers have been well-publicised online with anecdotes of longer working hours and lesser staff looking after patients' needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And at what percentage must manning levels not fall below to ensure an optimal level of healthcare is rendered to patients?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be important for the Government to lay out its short- or medium-term solution to this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I asked the Ministry to share its manpower recruitment plans and the additional doctors, nurses and allied health workers required, in view of our COVID-19 endemic strategy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The number must also accommodate the prospect of other future contingencies including any Disease X which is likely to overwhelm our medical services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of Omicron, future potential variants and surges, what is the recruitment plan for medical manpower that can sustain us through COVID-19 and, more generally, for the longer term?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has MOH develop a roadmap or a plan with public healthcare institutions to make up for the attrition in healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, I recently filed Parliamentary Questions on junior doctors' working conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some overseas studies do show that work hour reforms are not necessarily tied to adverse patient outcomes and that 80 hours is more than what is necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can study this locally before making changes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While it is understandable that hours are frontloaded in a junior doctor's career, so they are exposed to a variety of cases and have experience of disease progression and so on, recent reports of burnout are very concerning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Burnout harming doctors' well-being can impact patient care.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lack of work-life balance may also push well-trained healthcare workers to work in other countries or industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must also ensure that there is no under-reporting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand from my past Parliamentary Question that MOH has indicators showing that there is no systemic under-reporting, but anecdotal feedback suggests that this still happens to some extent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In cases where under-reporting or lack of compliance is found, let us move fast to study lapses and ensure manpower is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, I would like to suggest that MOH mandates concrete steps to shorten the time spent handing over and peripheral duties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 24-plus-hour duty is taxing and reducing administrative time will allow junior doctors to obtain sufficient rest before their next shift.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, it is clear that COVID-19 has complicated matters, especially for our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Due to exigencies of service, many are required to cover one another – sometimes at the last minute – work a bit longer, do a bit more and these may add up to less rest time or family time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The increase in the number of patients, coupled with rising expectations from patients and their family members for high quality care and service, may be the push factors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Hospital visitation, limited by COVID-19, may also have resulted in heightened frustration from some of the patients’ families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We expect them to care and smile, but do we care and smile back?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 situation merely spotlighted the hard work that they have always, always put in.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, we must ensure that they come to work energised, feel protected and respected by both colleagues and stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I declare that I work in a hospital.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, MOH called for help to support the COVID-19 operations as healthcare facilities find themselves overwhelmed by the Omicron wave.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As such, can we do more to encourage young Singaporeans to take up a career in healthcare so we can become more self-sufficient in the long term?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How can we better support workers who would want to have a mid-career conversion to healthcare?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to retain the senior talents that we have as they are key to training the next generation of workers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: To do so, employee well-being and working environment are important.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: During the pandemic, healthcare workers are also feeling the strain of more work and longer hours.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Would these be more effective in encouraging Singaporeans to consider a career in healthcare?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, how can we leverage workplace improvement, automation and digitalisaton to improve the delivery of healthcare?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: How can we improve processes to ensure that more time is spent on tasks directly related to patient care instead of administrative processes while not sacrificing patient safety?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a breast surgeon in private practice and my role as the elected President of Singapore Medical Association.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: In recent months, there have been articles in the news and letters to the Forum page highlighting the abuse of healthcare workers in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Twenty-five months of COVID-19 have placed immense social pressures on every single one of us.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: But being stressed should not be an excuse for patients to take on abusive behaviour towards healthcare workers or anyone for that matter.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I am glad that there is increasing awareness of this longstanding problem.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Healthcare professionals place patients at the heart of all we do and service before self.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: But when it comes to abuse, it becomes a really difficult thing to express how one feels abused without feeling guilty of being derelict in our duty.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: If healthcare workers are given the training to recognise it and the organisational support to be able to call out abusive and manipulative behaviours from patients or their families, it will give us all more protection, peace of mind and the strength to keep on doing what we love best.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Before you worry that healthcare workers over-react and claim that every patient complaint is an abuse, let me share two real-life examples.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: One, after a routine, uneventful surgery, on the day of discharge, a patient’s children demanded that the ward staff arrange for daily food delivery to the patient at home because they are all too busy to do so and said, I quote, "if anything should happen, it'll be your fault".

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Two, as a junior doctor, I once had to call a patient’s son to explain why a surgery had to be postponed for a second time – once, due to salt imbalance and once again due to unexpected fever.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: The son said, "You are lucky I am not there; otherwise, I will hang you, every single one of you".

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I am certain that many healthcare workers have their own stories of abuse to share.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Our professionalism mostly keeps us in check and stops us from posting on social media.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: And this is why there is such a skewed representation of cases of lapses in healthcare because healthcare workers would do open disclosures when a medical error has happened.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Yet, when the abuser is the patient, who can we talk to?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Yet, many healthcare workers may refrain from making an official Police report.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: They feel it is just a one-off event, they feel sorry that the patient is sick and not feeling well, or that the families are worried, thereby excusing such behaviour.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Another insight is that the type of emotional or verbal abuse that healthcare workers get can be just as elusive as that in an abusive relationship.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: We may not always recognise it, we just feel drained and guilty after meeting such patients or their families.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: We are afraid of speaking up, because patients hold the power here – a complaint to the senior management or their Member of Parliament may bring in undue social pressure to give in to unreasonable demands.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: For a doctor, an SMC complaint may take months or years to resolve, the media may splash a doctor's name across the main page and his or her reputation is ruined, even if found to be innocent later.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: There must be zero-tolerance of abuse on many different fronts.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: At the healthcare workers' level, one should have the professional option to terminate the patient-carer relationship after an encounter of abuse, with transfer of care to another provider.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: At the institution level, there needs to be clear protocols for reporting and management of abuse cases: such as making a Police report, making CCTV evidence available and with calling of witnesses.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: As a country, we can all play a part to be courteous and kind to one another, to give basic respect and human decency.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: My vision for Singapore – and even the world – is for us to be kinder, sensible towards and tolerant of differences.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Even as the world becomes divided over race, nationalities, vaccine status and so on, as individuals, let us be kind, embrace the Singapore Kindness Movement and practise it in our daily lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Everyone is going through their own personal hardships, which we may never fully understand.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I hope that, on the ground, we will see a greater push and enforcement of measures to ensure a safe environment.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Mr Adrian Tan, current President of the Singapore Law Society, shared in a LinkedIn post in December regarding healthcare worker abuse.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: That post had a wide discussion and engagement from professionals across different sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: Some, in service industries, brought up denial of service to abusive customers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: This is such a foreign concept to most local healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: But a few friends who have worked overseas have shared that, yes, their hospitals have provisions in place to turn away such visitors.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: These rare situations are typically for drunks or known drug addicts who come into the Emergency Department, not for a medical condition, but to demand drugs and were clearly abusive, such as screaming, shouting or even spitting at staff.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, this COVID-19 crisis has certainly tested the patience and resilience of our healthcare system and, most importantly, our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the above incentives, there were also not so nice news, whether in social media or even mainstream, on the mental challenges faced by this group of workers within the sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are also not sure how many of such workers that are facing similar workplace stress and challenges.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, quite a high number of reported resignations was recorded from healthcare staff due to the stress at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding these reported incidents, how does MOH engage the hospitals' management to identify the workers that are having mental health issues or stress during these challenging times?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What kinds of support are provided to any worker who comes forward?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For those who had resigned, were they our locals or foreigners who had decided to return home to be with their beloved families?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Besides that, I am not sure if MOH and MHA can also announce such incentives to all paramedics who have to receive and send COVID-19 patients either from their homes or even neighbourhood clinics to hospitals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, our doctors and nurses serving fellow Singaporeans to provide treatment and care in this never-ending battle against COVID-19 crisis deserve the fullest moral support in the course of their work.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I call on fellow Singaporeans to continue showing support for this group of workers in the battle during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Each simple smile and word of thanks to them will certainly help to boost their morale.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Chairman, mental health issues and well-being are a whole-of-society approach that spans across different age groups and segments of the community, from students to workers, youth to the elderly – and rightly so.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: In last year’s COS, MOH announced two task forces to strengthen support for mental health and well-being as a whole.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: First, Senior Minister of State Dr Janil Puthucheary shared that the Taskforce for Mental Health and Well-being will work on three areas: the development of a national strategy; creation of a resources webpage; and a competency training framework.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The second task force, announced by Minister Masagos, revolved around Child and Maternal Health and Well-being, to provide comprehensive support to women and their children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Like some say, "A healthy and happy mother has a healthy and happy child".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Investing more in our children is, inevitably, investing more in our mothers, too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Therefore, we must continue to provide the infrastructure and support: through greater access points within the community like the GP clinics and polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, it is heartening to see more open conversations acknowledging the stigma around mental health and the need to break this stigma.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our key task ahead is how to break the stigma, keep chipping away at it, keep shifting the needle, as a whole of society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As a first step, I believe we need to raise our collective awareness, knowledge and empathy on mental health.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, for instance, understanding that signs of distress do not mean a disorder per se.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A person who shows signs of anxiety, for example, may not have an anxiety disorder.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A person with low mood, low energy, feeling "depressed", may, nonetheless, not be facing a depressive disorder.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Symptoms and seeking help, counselling, therapy for these, do not mean there is a clinically-diagnosed condition.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And conversely, understanding that a person living with a clinical disorder may not actually show signs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: People around him or her may not even know.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we need to continue working at our collective understanding and sensitivity on mental health as an essential first step in tackling stigma as a society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because this translates into our words, the language that shapes our discourse.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Where our words are understanding, authentic, but sensitive and nuanced, it helps someone else to reach out to us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The right words can open up more doors for a person who may need help.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The right words can also help us to reach in, to open the doors of someone else's heart.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, building a kind, compassionate environment free of stigma starts with our words and our language.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And it also takes real skills, skills to truly listen and respond with empathy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In a dialogue I moderated, a youth in his early 20s made this important point.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: He suggested that older students in higher education should all have a chance to learn such skills.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This would better equip students to provide peer support and, indeed, a strong tapestry of peer support is also key to tackling stigma.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Peer support can be that first net to catch and embrace persons dealing with mental health challenges.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this should not just be for youths.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We should strive to build up a state of peer support that permeates through a person's life course, through youth, as a working adult and, importantly, as a senior, when challenges such as isolation become particularly salient.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But peer support cannot replace professional help, when it is needed.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this respect, for professionals working with children, the obligation to inform is a particular challenge at times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It deters some children who need help from coming forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the interplay with the existing stigma adds to the complexity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is hard work for mental health professionals who are working with parents and children to see how best they can support each child and every case is different.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But where there are successes, we should get these stories out, so that we can encourage more children and more parents who need help to come forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Stigma and other crucial issues relating to better mental health and care are a long journey that takes all of us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the formation of the Interagency Taskforce on Mental Health and Well‐being is a strong signal of the Government's commitment to this very important journey.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I look forward to an update by the task force about its work later.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Chairman, I initially filed this cut under the Prime Minister's Office because I am raising the recommendation for a permanent Mental Health Office under PMO.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Multiple studies and public polls, such as those by the Institute of Mental Health, SG Mental Health Matters and other community groups have shown that factors impacting mental health are complex and cut across many domains of our lives.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Mental well-being is something of national concern, which straddles many Ministries.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Adult mental health and well-being will require a different approach as compared to that of youth and seniors.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: In addition to age differences, there is also a need to address the mental well-being of people of different backgrounds, such as teachers, social workers, ex-offenders and victims of scams, just to name a few.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: To touch all bases requires close coordination between Ministries, as well as adequate authority and resources to be able to roll out the initiatives.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Mental health issues are something that will not go away.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: We should not invest in mental health only as a COVID-19 response and recovery but as something permanent to create better physical health outcomes, stronger families, increased economic productivity and long-term growth and development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, COVID-19 has impacted our mental health too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But 81.8% of participants said that they will be willing to seek professional help.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am therefore concerned that the current MediSave cap is insufficient for low-income individuals that may wish to seek help but may not be able to afford it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, only mental illnesses listed under the 20 chronic diseases under the Chronic Disease Management Programme entitle a patient to pay using his MediSave account.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To allow greater accessibility to psychiatric care in the community, the cap can be reviewed considering that on average, consultation fees in the private sector is over $100 per session, excluding the course of medication.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Increasing the amount allowable under MediSave may also allow patients more flexibility to consider seeking consultation with doctors in private hospitals as the wait time may be too long in structured hospitals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can perhaps, set a cap of a maximum number of sessions per year, for example, up to five.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, from FY2016 to FY2018, our public and total healthcare expenditure remained constant at 2.1% and 4.1% of our GDP respectively, approximately, but has since increased.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For comparison, Japan spends 9.3%, Germany spends 10.7% and the OECD average is about 8.8%.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: However, these two years have shown that we need a much more anti-fragile system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Healthcare workers, including nurses, ambulance staff, junior doctors, are overworked the moment colleagues begin falling ill or are told to stay at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I believe the Government understands that it needs to spend more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We see this in plans for upcoming infrastructure, like new polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would suggest that public mental health and dental care also needs to expand a lot faster than the headline rate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For mental health, I was told in a Parliamentary Question reply, that the number of psychologists here is only increasing by 4% annually.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is also not easy to qualify as a psychologist.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: From conversations with my constituents in the Serangoon ward of Aljunied GRC, the waiting time to see a public sector mental health professional or dentist can be long.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For such conditions, intervening early is important to limit further health or social consequences.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The age profile of applicants are largely seniors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a member of the PAP Seniors Group, I am concerned about these rising numbers and will speak on co-locating hemodialysis centres for added convenience and the promotion of alternative treatments plans to cope with the anticipated increase in caseloads.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am heartened to know that NKF has been working with MOH to build more centres for hemodialysis at HDB void decks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition to building dialysis centres closer to the community, a co-location with other medical facilities such as polyclinics can enhance patients' care.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, dialysis patients often need wound care and can seek such treatments at the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, co-locating a dialysis centre within transportation hubs can significantly reduce patients' travelling time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These forms of co-location provide better overall care outcomes as patients can now seek complementary treatments and greater convenience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At large, there is an increasing demand for Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT) on a national and global level.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, current hemodialysis treatments are unlikely to meet demand due to inherent constraints and there is a need to look for alternatives beyond community satellite hemodialysis.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alternatives include promoting peritoneal dialysis, which is a home-based treatment where patients can carry out treatment themselves in the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Peritoneal dialysis also allows for more flexibility, enabling patients to better fit dialysis into their lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite peritoneal dialysis being a viable alternative to hemodialysis, most patients are still choosing HD as a dialysis treatment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it is of paramount importance that we strengthen our public education on peritoneal dialysis treatments and empower healthcare providers to promote these alternative treatments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As close to 70% of kidney failure is a result of diabetes, we need to strengthen the link between diabetes and kidney failure in public education messages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lifestyle modifications are the best way to prevent deterioration of one’s kidney function.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upstream intervention and prevention are key to dealing with the anticipated increase of numbers of patients requiring dialysis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Mr Chairman, in Singapore, many healthcare providers leveraged on telehealth to remotely monitor at-risk patients’ conditions during COVID-19, when they were discouraged from visiting the hospitals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: With the current healthcare crunch, telemedicine is a solution to do more with less.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: This is especially so considering that many healthcare professionals find their time taken up by administrative work, which could be better used on clinical work and delivering better bedside care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The polyclinics continue to be crowded with patients, especially seniors, many of whom who are not familiar with telehealth, despite being the group that would benefit most from it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Yet, with the convenience brought about by digitalisation, security always seems to be the trade-off.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But this must not be the case, given the highly sensitive nature of healthcare data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The World Economic Forum warned that more needs to be done to strengthen healthcare cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Serious ransomware attacks could jeopardise the timely delivery of quality healthcare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The increase in our Budget expenditure was largely attributed to the costs associated with caring for an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The instructor-led fitness and exercise group workouts around the island by the Health Promotion Board is part of the Action Plan for Successful Ageing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: It gave an outlet for seniors to stay physically and socially active.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: During the pandemic, these exercises took a step back.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: For two years, we encouraged our seniors to stay home for their health and safety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Not everyone was able to switch to electronic means of socialising and exercising.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: What are the tangible methods to measure the success of the programme?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Even though the Ministry has committed more resources to improve the healthcare infrastructure, there are other areas of opportunity that require resources to grow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We need to improve our home-based care, caregiving and ageing in the community to free up resources from the public hospitals and clinics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: By leveraging on digitalisation, we can use telecare to reduce crowds in our healthcare institutions and provide more accessible healthcare in the community and convenience to patients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: A better relationship between seniors and GPs, and allowing seniors to choose their GPs, can help seniors manage their chronic health conditions better.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: And, as I have spoken in my Budget speech, the palliative care sector is in need of more resources for development.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: As Singaporeans live longer, there is a higher likelihood of suffering from more chronic health complications and severe illness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: These can bring about rather immense suffering, physically and emotionally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Palliative care plays a significant role in helping a patient maintain their dignity and peace at the end-of-life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I urge the Government to commit more resources to this.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Employment has generally been recognised as being good for health, as it provides for a sense of purpose, a social life and financial independence, which are crucial in old age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: A senior-friendly workplace will contribute many more productive years to a senior's health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I hope the Ministry can have more cross-collaboration with MOM to introduce more targets and programmes to get companies in Singapore to hire senior workers and make their workplace more senior-friendly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Successful ageing in Singapore should be a multi-pronged approach that involves self-reliance of seniors, partnerships with stakeholders, such as employers, and empowerment of family to care for their seniors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was targeted at seniors living alone who could enrol in the service and receive support, medication reminders and tele-befriending, if needed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Has the number of sign-ups remained promising after four years?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We also know that language barriers tend to be a challenge in bringing care to our seniors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Has there been feedback on whether this was also an obstacle in Careline and what steps have been taken to bridge that?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I gather that how Careline works is not necessarily by sending someone down to the senior who calls but also by linking them up with relevant agencies and community partners to provide more well-rounded support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is hard to quantify the success of holistic support though.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Perhaps, one way to measure efficacy would be to think of how Careline has helped expedite seniors' access to emergency responses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is but one among a buffet of tele-medical services that seniors and other vulnerable citizens can choose from when they are in distress.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Other 24-hour hotlines like the IMH's Mental Health Helpline.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Eldercare centres also conduct check-in calls to seniors in need of support, as does the Silver Generation Office, albeit with a more targeted approach.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There are also support hotlines operated by independent counselling centres and the National Care Hotline offering pandemic-related psychological support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: With so many different options, are seniors made sufficiently aware of the range of support that they can access, or is there some scope for a rationalisation exercise without drop in the quality of care?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the Government envisage expanding Careline and rolling it out to more seniors?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We at the PAP Senior Group are watching this review closely and with much anticipation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While MOH continues with the review, I hope MOH can consider the following.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, once Omicron subsides, decisively change the SMMs to encourage the revival of wellness activities conducted by the grassroots and by senior activity centres.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is a point that my colleague, Mr Yip Hon Weng, mentioned before.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, put a renewed focus on preventive health campaigns against diabetes, cancer, stroke and mental health.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, accelerate the efforts of Queenstown Health District and quickly scale up beyond Queenstown and hopefully, the whole of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Four, introduce fresh ideas to encourage more seniors to come forth for health screenings.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And five, enhance the scope of healthcare screening to detect and resolve more types of preventable and degenerative diseases and conditions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Given that we have transited to living with COVID-19 and most of our seniors are vaccinated and more anti-COVID-19 treatments are available, can MOH also share and elaborate on the current thinking on how to best care for our seniors' health and well-being moving forward?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While some seniors are raring to resume activities, some have retreated and gotten used to staying home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This leads to significant deterioration in mental acuity, emotional and physical well-being.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, I always remember Uncle Lee to be a jovial and active senior who loved to organise day trips for residents and tell me stories.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And I would see him with a big smile on his face at our community events.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since the pandemic, I saw little of him as he stayed home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Each time I saw him, he was less engaging and slower to react.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In January this year, I visited him again and he just sat in his chair, unable to recognise me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have also met other seniors who have aged so much faster in these two years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of them were pleased when I visited them and as we chatted, they broke down in tears as they articulated how lonely they felt.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must not let our seniors retreat into isolation and wither alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What more can be done to compensate for this "vacuum"?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: As our population ages and family sizes decline, more seniors are likely to have only themselves or their spouses to support them in their old age and many may require community care at some point in time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: During the Budget debate last year, I strongly supported the Community Care Apartment model piloted at the Harmony Village at Bukit Batok.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I am glad to hear from the MND's COS session yesterday that more of such Community Care Apartments (CCAs) will be launched and I hope MND will spread them island-wide to benefit more seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: A related issue that I hope to raise is incorporating senior care services in new BTO projects with flexi 2-room flats.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: During my walkabouts to newly completed BTO projects in the Buangkok Crescent estate of Jalan Kayu, which consist of mixed room types of between 2- to 5-room flats, I noticed that the flexi 2-room flats are mostly occupied by seniors living alone or with their spouse only, many of whom have chosen to downgrade to a smaller flat in their advanced years, mostly in their 70s and 80s.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: BTO projects in newer estates consist predominantly of younger families and the social and community services around then tend to cater to their needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: In fact, if more inter-generational community services that cater to both social and health well-being of our younger and older residents together, it will be beneficial to the community as a hope.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Mr Chairman, in my COS cut last year, I raised the concern of maternal health of mothers and its impact on their children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: With our birth rate continuing to slide, every child born is precious to us.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Ensuring the health of mothers and their children is hence a priority that needs our continued efforts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I am glad to hear that MOH has developed a Child and Maternal Health and Well-being Strategy to provide comprehensive support to women and their children, spanning from pre-conception to youths aged 18.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: These are formative years with many critical milestones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I hope to have more updates on what the new initiatives are and how the strategy will address health needs and mitigate risk factors of mothers and children in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: One emerging risk that I would like to highlight is on children's screen time usage and addictions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: COVID-19 has intensified the usage of technological devices for communication and entertainment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: A study done in 12 countries on those aged eight- to 36-month-old showed that children's screen time increased during COVID-19 lockdown relative to before.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: The study found that many caregivers would have to juggle both caring for children working from home had limited access to other activities to occupy their children's time and this resulted in screen time being the only way to occupy their children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I also note another Straits Times' article published just last Sunday, introducing a set of guidelines by a workgroup led by KK Women's and Children's Hospital (KKH), aimed at supporting parents to instil better daily habits from birth, helping young children get enough sleep and reducing screen time exposure to improve their health and well-being in the long term.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: As we move to an endemic Singapore, I hope that more outdoor activity options will become the preferred choices of our children and youth to participate in so that screen time will not dominate their days.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I spoke extensively on the need to lift the restrictions on egg freezing for singles.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: More Singaporeans are getting married later and having children later, which may have some impact on fertility.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
