text: Individuals, such as Mdm Lalitha have also stood up to promote health within the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Believing that mental well-being is just as important as physical health, she co-founded Club2Care in 2017, a non-profit organisation to create awareness of the importance of mental well-being and seeking help when needed within the Indian community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Club2Care is a supporter of HPB’s "It's OKAY to reach out" campaign for good mental well-being.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Other than keeping the general population healthy, MOH is adopting a whole-of-Government approach to provide holistic support to women as well as their partners and families for better population health outcomes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Minister Masagos and Senior Minister of State Janil shared on the Child and Maternal Health and Well-being Strategy to give our young a head start.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Please allow me to elaborate on some of our communications and engagement efforts under the Strategy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over the course of last year, HPB has conducted focus group discussions and in-depth interviews with parents-to-be, fathers, mothers, medical and social service professionals to gain insights to their needs and preferred type of support.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is a one-stop evidence-based resource portal providing local health information.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Resources are broken down into actionable steps that parents can adopt for children and youths' health and well-being.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This addresses feedback from couples and parents about being “lost” in the varied opinions that are available online and consolidates reliable information in one place.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Parents like Ms Richelle and Mr Tan have given their stamps of approval for Parent Hub.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As parents of two children of different ages, Ms Richelle and Mr Tan shared that most online resources and e-books they referred to previously were age-specific and time consuming to go through, but they now can find all the information they need for their children under one portal.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As relatively new parents, my husband and I are also benefiting from the nuggets of information and quizzes on Parent Hub.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, we are working across various public agencies to coordinate programmes so that parents-to-be and parents are kept up to date, equipped with relevant information and skills, and can easily navigate programmes from different agencies.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, updates on school-based health programmes are also shared via MOE’s Parent Kit, a resource kit that parents can conveniently access digitally via the MOE’s Parent Gateway mobile application.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We understand Miss Cheng Li Hui had concerns about how we are supporting couples on fertility health.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are looking into supporting couples with ready access to evidence-based fertility health information to empower them to make fertility decisions and enable them to seek help when needed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also recognise the psychosocial impact that fertility treatments may have on couples and are exploring how we may better support them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our partners in the community have done good work to increase awareness on women’s health issues and promote healthier lifestyle practices amongst women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some of these partners like Breast Cancer Foundation, Singapore Cancer Society and Persatuan Pemudi Islam Singapura (PPIS) have been encouraging women to come forth for their recommended breast and cervical cancer screening tests.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Other partners, such as Osteoporosis Society Singapore, have been reaching out to the wider population, from Primary school students to adults and seniors, to increase awareness about bone health, osteoporosis and fall prevention.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This would strengthen our outreach efforts by bringing together all the members’ efforts, events and activities with the aim of getting women to take charge of their own health under a common umbrella.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are committed to celebrating our seniors and enabling them to live to their fullest potential in the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many seniors take pride in staying active and taking charge of their own well-being.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To support this, MOH actively onboard aged care facilities onto the new Eldercare Centre Service Model, where seniors can receive Active Ageing, Befriending and referral to Care services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling spoke about engagement with seniors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This model enabled seniors to remain connected to both care staff and other seniors even during the pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, Mdm Jarnail, who stays alone, has received continuous support and social engagement from the Blossom Seeds’ Eldercare Centre care staff.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With their support, she continues to engage in both physical and virtual activities, such as the National Day Intergenerational Programme with schools.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She also participates in exercise sessions, where she made friends with other seniors and became healthier and more alert.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This enables her to stay socially connected and healthy, while her son works in the day.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are encouraged by these and many other positive stories and feedback received and are expediting the onboarding of more Eldercare Centres.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These will be accessible and located near both existing and new BTOs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling can be assured that we will provide care and support services for seniors, including those living in new 2-room Flexi flats.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Befriending is also a key part of the Eldercare Centres, especially for seniors staying alone.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will be complemented with outreach by the Silver Generation Ambassadors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, we provide tele-befriending and emergency response services to seniors through the "CareLine" social support hotline.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: CareLine runs 24/7 and is supported by call agents trained in vernacular languages.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Each month, we also receive around 30 calls that require emergency services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To reduce the burden on emergency services, call agents are trained to triage seniors’ conditions after a distress episode and provide remote assistance or activate non-urgent in-person assistance through nearby community providers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over the past few years, we have taken many steps to strengthen care initiatives for seniors in a comprehensive, accessible and cost-effective manner.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will share more details during the launch of the Refreshed Action Plan later this year.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of our seniors want to contribute meaningfully.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This may be through learning, volunteerism and employment.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One interesting project which emerged during our engagement sessions with Singaporeans was "Stories for Our Seniors".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through this initiative, seniors can volunteer to tell stories using their Mother Tongue Language.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This encourages the building of inter-generational bonds with younger Singaporeans and the imparting of life learnings and values through recounting their own experiences, history and heritage.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These active interactions can help to address concerns raised by Ms Tin Pei Ling about the deterioration in mental acuity, emotional and physical well-being that seniors may face during the pandemic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Next, HPB and the People’s Association will also jointly roll out a new Health and Wellness Programme called "Live Well, Age Well" in our community nodes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to support seniors to age-in-place by increasing access to diverse home and community-based care options within an inclusive built environment.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This enables seniors to access affordable care options, even at the end-of-life and as they stay close to their families and friends.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will complement the public Community Care Apartment model.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Seniors can look forward to a continuum of care that supports their physical and mental well-being.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To conclude, MOH will continue to enhance upstream efforts to sharpen our preventive health strategy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are also committed to strengthening our support for couples before and throughout their parenthood journey and seniors to age well in their golden years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As the Government puts in place various measures and resources, we would also like to urge Singaporeans to take greater ownership of your health today and make positive strides, so that together, we can all live better, for longer.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, I want to thank Members for all your questions and your cuts, and my MOH colleagues for addressing most of them and stitching up most of the cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is a remaining batch mostly on preventive care, which I will address.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, please allow me to start with a tribute to our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For over two years, they have toiled and fought against the COVID-19 virus, putting themselves in harm’s way, undergoing tremendous stress and, even as we speak, they are keeping our population safe and life in Singapore as normal as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At MOH, we have been doing whatever we can to support them, ensuring sufficient PPE, prioritising them for vaccinations, decanting as many patients as possible to COVID-19 Treatment Facilities and out of the hospitals, persuading the public to undertake self-recovery if they are infected and experience mild or no symptoms, and imposing the very difficult "no visitor" rule in hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More than these clinical protections, we must stand up for them, against the abuse they suffer under the hands of a small minority of our population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH’s instructions to the leaders of our public health institutions are clear – we must always protect them against abuse and insults.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is something that we must also do as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are now good indications that the Omicron transmission wave has peaked and starting to subside.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With that, I hope, not too long from now, healthcare workers will finally have a well-deserved and lasting respite.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The men and women of the healthcare sector, are brave, dedicated, committed, big-hearted, professional and they deserve all the support, respect and understanding that we can give.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will address the questions on preventive care from several Members – Dr Tan Wu Meng, Ms Ng Ling Ling, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Mr Henry Kwek and maybe others.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a journey started more than 10 years ago by previous Health Ministers, to focus on health, rather than cure.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: During this journey, we have built a very robust foundation for the Singapore healthcare sector.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The changes I am about to announce are only possible because of all these past achievements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, from 2010 to 2020, the capacity and capability of the healthcare system have been strengthened significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Senior Care Centre capacity expanded almost four times.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a result, the number of doctors per thousand population improved from 1.8 to 2.6 and that for nurses gone up from 5.8 to 7.4.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These ratios are similar or higher than most Asian regions and territories, normalised to the proportion of older people in the population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But they are lower than ratios in OECD countries, as observed by Ms Mariam Jaffar.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is due to a variety of reasons, including the population age profile, the model of care in different countries, between western countries and in Asia, and also the way western countries fund, subsidise and insure healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In terms of policies, we implemented MediShield Life and CareShield Life; we rolled out the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages; we introduced the Community Health Assist Scheme or CHAS.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In terms of structures, we established three healthcare clusters, centering around Singapore General Hospital (SGH), Tan Tock Seng Hospital (TTSH) and National University Hospital (NUH), each with significant economies of scale and capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Between 2015 and 2020, there are fewer readmissions into hospitals within 30 days after discharge, fewer U-turns, from 11.5% in 2015; 2020 – it came down, 10.7%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Response time to cardiac and stroke care at our hospitals have also improved.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, now, if you look across 204 countries in the world, Singapore had the highest life expectancy at birth – for men, at 83 years; and women, at 87 years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After 10 years of foundation laying, plus a pandemic crisis, it is time for us to take the next big step.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is urgency to this, because in the next 10 years, long after the COVID-19 dust has settled, we will have to tackle our biggest healthcare challenge since our nation began – the deteriorating health of our population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked what is driving cost increases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Currently, about one in seven residents in Singapore are seniors aged 65 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: An older person is more likely to fall sick or suffer from severe illnesses compared to a young person – it is a fact of life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We see this in our parents and grandparents and in time, we will feel it ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second driving force, which is quite aside from age, Singaporeans young and old, are, generally, getting less healthy, even after adjusting for age.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, in 2017, about two in 10 has high blood pressure.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2020, this has become about three in 10.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are more of us with high cholesterol, from about three in 10 to four in 10, and I am one of them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fortunately, for diabetes, the prevalence rate has been constant, likely due to our efforts in the War on Diabetes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first factor of ageing, that is due to the march of time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is very little we can do about.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second driving force due to deteriorating health, this is due to the will of people, of which there is plenty we can do about it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because deteriorating health is mostly a function of lifestyle – too sedentary, too much device time, too little exercise, too much sugar, salt and fat in our diet; and putting off looking after our health until it is too late.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And indeed, living unhealthily is often more carefree and often more enjoyable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we do not realise that we are paying for these instant gratifications by instalments, with our long-term health – bit by bit – until we realise the snowballing cost later in life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, a young person who is obese, or has high blood pressure or high blood sugar, he may feel all right now, but actually, he may be a walking "time bomb".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When he is older, there is a high chance of him being struck with a heart attack, stroke or require dialysis.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They snatch away from us quality of life and happiness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will burden family members and loved ones, emotionally and financially.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For this generation of seniors, many have several children, who can all chip in to help take care of them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And even so, it can be quite taxing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But people around my age, slightly older, slightly younger, we have fewer children and we are likely to live longer.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That means when we are in our 80s, 90s and if you are lucky, 100s.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you fall very sick, unable to walk, change, eat, shower, our children will be in their 50s or 60s and hopefully, they will be able to take care of us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even so, the two percentage-point increase in GST may not be sufficient given the rate at which healthcare costs are increasing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we also need to control costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have been doing so through bulk buying of drugs, using cost-effective treatments, better clinical procedures, right siting patients and moderating the buffet syndrome caused by healthcare insurance.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the more fundamental way to tackle cost is at its roots.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It would not reverse the impact of an ageing population, but it can reduce the rate of increase and "bend the cost curve" downwards in the long run.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will still slope upwards but we can bend it downwards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many doctors that I have spoken to have always wondered: how did a patient become so stricken with chronic illness?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why did not he make lifestyle adjustments when he was younger?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why only now that he comes to me when he is so sick?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I was younger, in my 30s and 40s, you feel almost invincible – you will never fall sick.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I did not feel the need to take care of my health too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, a doctor friend of mine kept nagging me to go for health screening. "Go for health screening." He sees me, he says, "Go for health screening." Since he is my friend, I listened to him.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, after the test, he found that I have quite high levels of cholesterol.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Based on my risk level, he performed further tests and found a very small calcium deposit in one of my heart arteries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, at his advice, I started taking some medication, adjusted my diet – nothing very austere.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have to cut down chilli crabs, prawns and sotong – not a huge sacrifice, as Mr Pritam Singh is acknowledging.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: No, I can still eat them once a month.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I just do not eat them every other day!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, eat in moderation but certainly not deprivation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If anyone wants to treat me to seafood, I will say yes!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I just went two weeks ago and my reading are now fine.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More importantly, because of early intervention, I probably averted a major heart bypass surgery when I become old, or worse, a heart attack that may kill me and distress my family and my loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We usually associate better healthcare with fascinating medical technology or heroics in the operating theatre like when we watch Grey's Anatomy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those are important but good health is more likely to come from an accumulation of the humdrum and the mundane, because as the saying goes, "prevention is better than cure." We need to, as Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Henry Kwek said, maintain health, rather than treat sickness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we are not called the Ministry of Sickness, but we are called the Ministry of Health!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The measures must be taken early, when the person is still healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It must identify the risk factors in our lives that will erode our health slowly and quietly, and then address these factors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It must be done in homes and in the community, not in hospitals or clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is best centred on the family doctors – in polyclinics and GP clinics – and less on surgeons and specialists in hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have worked out the broad plan but still finalising the details.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will outline five key components of the Healthier SG strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, mobilise our network of family physicians and family doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Studies have shown that people who go to only one family doctor consistently, are generally healthier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have fewer visits to the emergency department and fewer episodes of hospital care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is because the doctor and his care team know you well and can detect early signs of any problems in a timely and accurate way.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The family doctor can do for you what my friend has done for my chronic condition.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Go to doctor A for hypertension medicine, go to doctor B for cough and cold and get MC.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there is no one family doctor who knows our overall health condition and family health history well enough to be able to see the link between different care episodes, even across different family members.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we now have a golden opportunity to bring as many of our family doctors as possible into this long-term national public health programme – and that opportunity is made possible by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When we needed more people to get vaccinated against COVID-19, I personally wrote to the GPs and also to TCM practitioners and asked them for help.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, they heeded the call, explained the need for vaccinations and persuaded many of their patients to take the jab.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Throughout the pandemic, they served as the first port of call for people who fell sick and suspected that they might have been infected by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, during the Omicron wave, GPs took on an even greater role – they assessed the severity of patients coming to them, placed them on home isolation if they have mild symptoms and low risk and then supported their recovery, often by telemedicine.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And therefore, they demonstrated that rest and recovery at home is appropriate for many ailments and that telemedicine does work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our COVID-19 response would have been inadequate, even crippled, if not for the contributions of our family doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have been a key component of the national crisis response.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH has been working in partnership with GP clinics for some time, started by my predecessors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They also serve as Public Health Preparedness Clinics (PHPCs) during pandemics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: COVID-19 has deepened that partnership and now, we can leverage on this in order to implement Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can leverage GPs to attend to more patients, not for coughs and colds, but devoting time to provide preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH will support this, by building up the clinics' capabilities, such as telemedicine and IT systems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will work with the GPs to develop the skills of clinic healthcare team and forge partnerships with hospitals to deliver more integrated team-based care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second component of Healthier SG is healthcare plans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is especially useful if you are at risk of developing a chronic condition, like diabetes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To support residents to follow through with the care plans, we need to make them accessible, attractive, maybe even rewarding.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will conduct public and stakeholder consultations to work out these proposals and incorporate them in a White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am very sure there will be no shortage of ideas and we have heard several today from Members.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think we can implement them all, but we will try to put together a package that is compelling, attractive and which we can afford.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Perhaps, some ideas: preventive care consultations with family doctors and recommended health screenings could be made free or costing only a nominal sum.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Just to assure Dr Tan Yia Swam, this does not mean that GPs will not be paid, they will just be reimbursed elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Perhaps we can claim higher CHAS benefits for drugs if we go to the same doctor; perhaps we can tap on MediSave more for our care plan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Perhaps we can offer insurance premium discounts or vouchers if we diligently follow our care plans or even, better still, show good outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our third component is that we then need community partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Preventive care plans involve lifestyle adjustments, which need to happen outside of the clinics and in our living environments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They call these "social prescriptions", as opposed to drug prescriptions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We, therefore, need the support of agencies, many of them, Health Promotion Board, Agency for Integrated Care, People’s Association, SportSG, National Parks Board and community partners that oversee various social services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They run various activities and programmes in the community which we then get family doctors to tap on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, one analogy: if we have a major illness, we go to a doctor, the doctor often refers us to a few specialists or therapists.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in a preventive care plan, the family doctor may refer us to a qigong class, to a brisk walking group, or a community farming club, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We already have such collaborations on the ground – some Members have mentioned it – in Queenstown and Tampines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to roll out such initiatives across every town to make good health not just a matter for doctors in clinics, but for all of us in everyday life and places.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once the first three components are in place, we will roll out a national Healthier SG enrolment programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is when I mentioned by enrolling into Healthier SG, a resident will commit to see one family doctor and adopt one care plan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The national enrolment programme will be coordinated by our three healthcare clusters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, we will have to build up the participation base progressively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When HPB rolled out the latest season of the National Steps Challenge, it recruited 900,000 participants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We hope Healthier SG can be even more successful than that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to specifically highlight the importance of this collaboration between healthcare clusters and the family doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a very important nexus, because the family doctors will receive support from hospitals in looking after residents with more complex needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hospitals, after discharging a patient, can refer them back to the family doctor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is exactly what we did during COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It works and there will be seamless coordination and continuity of care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have taken a geographical approach to enrol residents because this will cater to the needs of the great majority because, today, about nine in 10 residents will visit a family doctor or hospital near their homes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can choose whether to enrol or not.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can choose who to enrol with, even doctors who are far away from your home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are a variety of reasons why some Singaporeans may decide to do that, because the clinic may be nearer to your workplace, near your parents’ place, or is a friend that you have known for many years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need the necessary support structures to make Healthier SG work and this is actually no small matter.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar asked for our workforce transformation plans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to build up and optimise our primary and community care workforce further.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But besides growing the number, we will further build up the competencies and skills of our healthcare workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For doctors, family medicine should feature even more strongly in the curriculum of our medical schools.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We now encourage new graduates not to become a specialist and do your residency straightaway but get exposed more broadly in medicine and build up confidence in dealing with chronic illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Postgraduate training in family medicine will be strengthened, too.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For nurses and other healthcare professionals, the potential for skills upgrading is even greater.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to broaden interdisciplinary training and empower them to practise at the highest level of their licences.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, once we roll out Healthier SG, I expect preventive care efforts to be implemented in communities and these efforts can be led by nurse clinicians and pharmacists, not necessarily by doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I foresee Healthier SG opening up many new job roles for our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Under the new system, the absolute budgets of each healthcare cluster will not be affected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, the budgets will go up a little bit.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What will change is the basis of calculating the budgets.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Appropriate surgeries, procedures and treatments will always be provided when required.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But with this shift in the basis of funding, there will be a natural incentive for hospitals to try to keep residents healthy through preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Complementing this new basis of funding is a set of KPIs, a set of health outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some salient indicators are quality of care, uptake of healthy lifestyles and habits, prevalence of chronic illnesses, cost effectiveness of treatments and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Family doctors in the frontline of Healthier SG will need good system and data support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They must have access to patients’ medical records.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They must have the IT tools to track their patients' conditions and progress over time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They must also be able to share their records with other healthcare providers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to work towards a scenario that no matter where you are receiving care, for example, at the GP or dental clinics, polyclinics, hospitals, SOCs, nursing homes, eldercare centres, the same data can be retrieved to support your care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why MOH has been enhancing and rolling out the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We then need to ensure that such data sharing is secured and users take greater responsibility for data access.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We would need new legislation to govern this and we intend to put in place a Health Information Bill in the next couple of years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, let me now say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, in the next few years, we will be putting in place a major healthcare reform.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will focus on preventive health care for two reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we get older, we will inevitably have more illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, Singaporeans are actually becoming more and more unhealthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we should do more, we do not do enough and vice versa, what we should do less, it is not sufficiently less.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not enough physical activity, not enough exercises on a daily basis, over-use of electronic gadgets, consuming too much sugar, salt and oil.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, there are more people with chronic diseases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we do not change our lifestyle and habits, we will suffer more illnesses in the next 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you are sick, your quality of life will be compromised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After retirement, you may have plans to try something new, or spend time with your family, but should you become sick, you will be unable to achieve your aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once we fall ill, we have to rely more on our families, children and grandchildren for simple daily living or medical expenses, and this will add to their burden.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Apart from this, the healthcare system will also be under more pressure, so will Government healthcare spending.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We know the saying "prevention is better than cure".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: TCM practitioners also often say that "illness is best treated at an early stage".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this requires lifestyle and diet changes, even before you fall sick.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Chinese idiom of “preparing for rainy days before the torrential rain” is most appropriate to use on healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, our top priority is to help you stay healthy, instead of going to the doctor only after you fall sick.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In any healthcare system, prevention and treatment are equally important.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will encourage middle-aged Singaporeans to sign up with their family doctor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After that, the family doctor will work with public hospitals to assist you in disease prevention and stay healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The doctor will also help you do health screening on a regular and scheduled basis and get you vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will work with community partners, including the People's Association and SportSG, to help you improve your eating habits and diet, quit smoking and do more exercises.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But preventive care means that you see a doctor, go for regular check-ins and even health coaching when you are feeling fine.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We tend to think "why do we see a doctor for no reason?".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To encourage people to do so, we need some incentives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Within the package, perhaps, preventive health screening can be free, or at a nominal cost.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Perhaps, more Medisave can be used to pay for medication.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Perhaps, if you stay healthy according to your family doctor’s care plan, there could be MediShield Life premium discount.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If your car is accident-free and no repair is needed, then your insurance premium will be reduced.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the strategy direction in place and with the support and cooperation of hospitals, family doctors and the public, we can all lead healthier and more fulfilling lives, and the elderly can enjoy their twilight years happily.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, a central issue of the Budget this year has been the increase of GST, because we need to meet the rising healthcare expenditure of an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthcare expenditure will increase because we are committed to make healthcare affordable to those who are sick by heavily subsidising healthcare bills.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After subsidy, there is still a remaining sum that needs to be paid.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can cover most of them through MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then there is still a smaller remaining sum, which the patient can pay through his MediSave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, it is important to understand that spending on health is quite different from spending on, say, education, which is always forward-looking, moulding the future of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthcare spending is critical, it is essential but mostly about treatment – trying to restore a sick person back to where he was in the past and, often, imperfectly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sometimes, we hear comments, including in this House, that healthcare spending is an investment in our people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we are honest with ourselves, we know it is not the same as education.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is driven by deteriorating health that can be prevented.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is often about paying for unwise lifestyle choices of our past.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But there is a component in our healthcare spending that is forward-looking and about investing in our future and, that is, preventive care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we are saying here is that as healthcare spending inevitably grows in the coming years, let us have the discipline to always set aside enough to invest in keeping our people healthy for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have been lucky to have a highly-trained and well-meaning doctor friend who nagged me and helped me.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I seek the support of Members to translate Healthier SG into a healthier Singapore population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, I thank the Minister for showing the healthier way forward.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Over the next 10 years, will new hospitals be built, just like the last 10 years that the Minister has just painted?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: So, if there are going to be new hospitals, how about the private sector-wise?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Will there be new private hospitals as well?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: So, that is something I would like to know.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Second, since we need more medical manpower, from that itself, will current medical school enrolment numbers increase?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There are many Singaporeans who aspire to study medicine but just because they cannot get into our local medical schools, many of the parents have to spend lots of money to send them overseas.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Third, regarding the S+3M framework, I agree with the Minister that that is the bedrock for healthcare financing now.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: But as healthcare cost goes up, how will this structure change?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When was the last time we reviewed this framework?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member is right to describe that it is a bedrock and it is also very robust, designed and evolved over the years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I took Members through the process of subsidy; insurance; remaining, use your own savings in MediSave which is also contributed by your employers; and then, for those with low income, MediFund.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But having said that, even today, as Members read out your cuts, there are several suggestions: how to activate them better to help make things easier for the population to take care of their health.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will take them in, we will continue to review and, as you can see, over the years, the rules are always being refreshed, improved and strengthened to better support Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: He asked about whether there would be further hospitals, further healthcare capacity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We watch the issue of healthcare capacity quite closely and, as Minister Ong Ye Kung has laid out, the key thing that we want to achieve going forward is better utilisation of the healthcare capacity that we have, integration into the community facilities that we have and where care can be sited outside of the hospital, if possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Studies have demonstrated quite clearly that this is going to be better if we can go upstream and better integrate recovering patients into the community.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we will watch the need for healthcare capacity quite closely, but we are hoping that the solution to the healthcare capacity issue is not just more and more acute care hospitals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are hoping to be able to reduce the need for them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the point on medical schools, indeed, medical manpower is important and a lot of people who are interested in pursuing a career in healthcare, we need healthcare workers from many, many degrees and many, many domains and many, many disciplines, and we would encourage people who are interested in a career in healthcare to explore a wider variety of possibilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I will just add a couple of points about the possibility of increasing medical school intake.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to monitor the manpower pipeline needed to support our healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And, as I have said earlier in my speech, we are looking at care model changes and how care delivery in hospitals ought to be changed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is not just going to be a single-track increase in numbers to meet needs but, actually, evolving a model so that we can do more with less.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And also the manpower projections will change based on the kind of care model that we are going to put in place in the hospitals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, I welcome the Healthier SG plan and working closer with GPs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: First, how will MOH measure the outcomes of success under this plan, especially since some of the interventions for seniors involve not so much medical care but rather social prescribing like exercise activities and so on and also working with social care agencies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Second, under this plan, will we encourage GPs to work together to share resources and for better demand aggregation to serve residents better?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I can tell you, as of now in MOH, we have developed such a long list of KPIs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to whittle it down to a more manageable set and, in time, I think we can share them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: I think the Healthier SG initiative is a very exciting development.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: As a dentist myself, I would also like to say that oral health is very important.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: It is intricately linked with good health and dental treatment is also quite expensive.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: So, may I know if this initiative will be extended to preventive dentistry as well?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: And is the Ministry planning to engage with the dental fraternity for the White Paper?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should inform Members that, in Singapore, for our young children below 12, we have one of the best oral health in the world and that is because of a very strong collaboration between MOH and MOE schools.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we were in Primary schools, we all dreaded the dental nurse coming into the classroom and reading out our names, because that means we would be going to the dentist.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But because of that, preventive care was done and executed very well for children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As we get older, bad habits set in and then dental hygiene and dental health deteriorate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, actually, the dental programme is a very good story about how effective preventive health or preventive care can be.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As the Minister observed, preventive healthcare has been a long journey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: HPB was founded in 2001 and we have been spending, I think, about $300 million a year for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will that be factored into the preventive healthcare plan going forward?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My second clarification is to Senior Minister of State Dr Koh.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just wanted to confirm what he said on the COVID-19 Healthcare Award for cleaners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I actually filed a Parliamentary Question on 14 February about whether cleaners were eligible for the COVID-19 Healthcare Award.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Healthier SG has been something we had been talking about for the last few months.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When I came to MOH in May last year, my first speech was about preventive care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I spoke to the healthcare community and the leaders of both private and public healthcare institutions, from then on, we have been talking about Healthier SG and consulting many people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What I announced today, in the healthcare sector, it is not a secret – except the name "Healthier SG" which we came up with a few weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the capitation model, IT system, preventive care, enrolment process are some things we have been talking about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I am not surprised that Mr Leon Perera filed an Adjournment Motion talking about this topic, because it is a very live topic within the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But when he mentioned the outcomes going the other way, I think that argument is counter-factual.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Imagine if we had not had HPB, imagine if we had not had "Step Challenge", imagine if we had not had the Primary Care Network (PCN), Public Health Preparedness Clinics (PHPCs) – I think that the outcome today would be far worse.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because we know what drove unhealthy populations are lifestyle, food, devices, sedentary lifestyle, all kinds of things that we are also guilty of.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But in the last 10 years, could we have, as he mentioned, thought deeply about it and come out with Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the ideas would have been there, execution would not be ready.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It took 10 years, more than 10 years of work from my predecessors: set in place the structure, three clusters; put in place the basic IT system, without the IT system you cannot implement this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Think through the funding process, communicate and talk to the clusters, build up the PCN structure, so that we have a basis to work on now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That 10 years of hard work enabled us to implement Healthier SG today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think we need to get that perspective correct.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Indeed, in the healthcare sector, many have been thinking that is very important to pivot to primary care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: And community care is a very important part of managing our ageing population, with a growing chronic disease burden.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I know there will be more consultations and a White Paper later on, but I hear Minister mention the National Health SG enrolment programme would likely be through the three clusters.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I am wondering for residents who may have GPs that they have been seeing that is outside the cluster, would they be allowed to choose and would they still get the potential incentives?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: In some countries that have similar systems, they have, in fact, allowed residents to have up to a choice of two GPs because a lot are working; so, they have a GP when they are in their workplace and one nearer their homes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: The second clarification I have is that, when I speak with my senior residents about where they get chronic care, their chronic disease management and when I ask them about whether they go to the nearby GP clinics, many of them still feel that the out-of-pocket expense can be higher than if they go to a Public Health Institution.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: So, I just wanted to check whether that is an area of focus during the White Paper consultation?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the Member feels that out-of-pocket expenses for consultation is an issue, by all means, let us know.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: I want to thank Senior Minister of State Dr Koh for the reply that MOH will monitor the situation of TPAs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: But I have done the research and I am sure that in 2016, Mr Desmond Choo raised a Parliamentary Question and the reply then by Mr Chee Hong Tat was that MOH will monitor the situation regarding TPAs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam
text: So, in these five to six years, what have we understood about the situation?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I said in my reply, we will continue to watch this, but we will be happy to also engage with the Singapore Medical Association (SMA) to see if they have insights on areas that we need to focus a bit more attention on.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Which is why our emphasis always has been that the GP entering into a contract with a service provider ought to be clear that the boundaries of ethics and ethical behaviour ought to be observed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Otherwise, it is very hard for us to police every single private contract between the GP and a third-party provider.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think that the principle must be observed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But if there are unsavoury practices that GPs have engaged in and if SMA is aware, we will probably take some investigative action and advise the relevant parties to not undertake such actions to the detriment of patients.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As we evolve the primary healthcare landscape based on Healthier SG, some of these arrangements between GPs and third-party service providers, like TPAs, may also need to be relooked at as well to see how they should reshape themselves in the larger landscape of primary care changes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We still have some time before the Guillotine Time of 5.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One of the reasons that the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has rejected the Budget is that we want the Government to concentrate more on cutting healthcare cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We hope that this plan would realise that in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have three supplementary questions with regards to the plan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is, a lot of feedback from the ground about our current healthcare system is, not so much of the poor being not given medical, healthcare services or treatment, but more of the middle class who can pay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When they get into a healthcare situation, it somehow drains their finances very fast, although we talk about S+3Ms and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The first question I want ask is: will the new plan that the Ministry is coming out with take care of that as well, that means give more relief to the middle class?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There are many, many areas like, for example, they do not get so much subsidies compared to the lower income, certain medicines are not included and so on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second point is that the Minister mentioned about outcome.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is a concept in healthcare for quite some time already.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I look forward to seeing how the Minister is going to present the plan that take cares of that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One of the things that I thought of in the past when I was running a healthcare fund, that we have also talked about, is how to incentivise the —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Excuse me, Mr Leong, a clarification is really about you raising a question regarding what a person has already said.

speaker: The Chairman
text: It is not a licence to give another speech.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will give you some leeway, please ask your points two and three quickly, so that the Minister can reply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the second point is: can the Minister enlighten us a bit more on what kind of outcome, what kind of incentive, just a little bit, how is it related to incentivising the individual patient to take more care about his health?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The third point is: healthcare is a very resource-intensive thing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have read that overseas, people are activating community resources to help.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, in Singapore today, when I walk the ground, there are a lot of Singaporeans who are prematurely retired.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Are there plans, in the plan that the Minister is putting up, to tap into this resource?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Leong said three questions, but I counted quite a number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, he said PSP recommend "cutting" healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not the right description of what we are doing here.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we are not "cutting" healthcare cost per se.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When treatments, operations, surgeries are required, they will be given.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the middle class, how will Healthier SG take care of their current issues, where if they have a catastrophic illness, it will wipe out a lot of their cash?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We want to help every Singaporean take care of their own health, through Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Outcomes delivered by our healthcare system, is not a new concept.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is a major outcome, delivered over the decades.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we will continue to focus Healthier SG on delivering right outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But now, because of the design of that programme, we have to look at specific outcomes that we are driving at.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How many percent taking up enrolment, taking up healthcare plan, how many percent have one single doctor, what is the subscription of doctors into this plan, how many doctors are in our national IT system, because those are essential.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, some of these outcomes, drivers have to be captured as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think I have answered that in my speech, which is we will have a consultation, we will put in the package, we will describe the package in the White Paper to be tabled in this House later.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think I have answered all his questions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If there are no further clarifications, may I invite Dr Tan Wu Meng, if you like, to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Mr Chairman, we have seen around the world challenges from the pandemic and what has been at stake.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: What has happened to those healthcare systems that broke under pressure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And some of this is through the policies and effort of the MOH team – the civil servants, the Director of Medical Services (DMS), everyone working, policies that lay the groundwork for healthcare workers to be able to do their best as far as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: The Healthier SG announcement is significant and will be an important part of the next bound for Singapore healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: It will shape us a generation from now.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: So, I would like to thank Minister Ong, Second Minister Masagos, our two Senior Ministers of State, Senior Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon, Senior Minister of State Dr Janil Puthucheary, Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu, our Permanent Secretaries, our DMS – the whole team at MOH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And in particular, I want to again thank every single healthcare frontliner, whose effort and sacrifice has kept Singapore afloat and in one piece through this pandemic.
